lessons.title: Seed Selection and Rootstock Varieties
lessons.body: When you grow citrus from seed, the tree may not be the same as the parent, and it will take many years to fruit. That is why farmers use rootstocks. A rootstock is the bottom part of the tree that provides the roots. The top part, called the scion, is the variety you want fruit from. Choosing the right rootstock is key. In Africa, common rootstocks include Rough Lemon, which is vigorous and drought-tolerant but susceptible to some diseases; Sour Orange, which is hardy and tolerates calcareous soils but is sensitive to tristeza virus; and Cleopatra Mandarin, which is resistant to tristeza and produces good quality fruit. For sandy soils, Rough Lemon is often used. For heavy soils, Sour Orange may be better. Always buy rootstock seeds from a certified supplier to avoid diseases. Sow seeds in a nursery bed with well-drained soil, rich in organic matter. Plant seeds 1-2 cm deep, spaced 5 cm apart. Water regularly. Seeds germinate in 2-4 weeks. When seedlings are 15-20 cm tall, they are ready for grafting. Remember, rootstock choice affects tree size, fruit quality, and pest resistance. Talk to extension officers or other farmers to know what works in your area. Always keep records of your rootstock and scion sources.

lessons.title: Grafting Techniques for Citrus
lessons.body: Grafting joins a scion (the fruiting variety) to a rootstock. The most common method for citrus is the cleft graft, done when the rootstock is 1-2 cm thick. First, cut the rootstock horizontally about 20-30 cm above the soil. Make a vertical slit about 3 cm deep in the center of the cut surface. Prepare the scion: take a healthy shoot of the desired variety, about 10-15 cm long, with 2-3 buds. Cut the bottom of the scion into a wedge shape, about 3 cm long. Insert the wedge into the slit so the cambium layers (the green layer under the bark) of scion and rootstock meet on at least one side. Wrap the union tightly with grafting tape or polythene strip to hold it and prevent drying. Cover the scion and union with a plastic bag to keep humidity high. Place the grafted plant in a shaded area. After 2-3 weeks, check for new growth. Remove the bag gradually. Grafting is best done during active growth, usually at the start of the rainy season. Tools needed: sharp knife, grafting tape, plastic bags, and pruning shears. Keep tools clean with alcohol to avoid disease. Success rate can be 70-90% if done properly. Grafting allows you to grow many trees with the same good fruit quality and disease resistance.

lessons.title: Budding Methods and Timing
lessons.body: Budding is another way to propagate citrus. It involves inserting a single bud from the desired variety into the rootstock. The most common method is T-budding or shield budding. Do this when the rootstock is about 1 cm thick, usually 6-12 months after sowing. The best time is when the bark slips easily, which is during active growth, often in the rainy season. To T-bud, make a T-shaped cut on the rootstock about 15-20 cm above the ground. Cut a bud from the scion with a piece of bark (the shield) about 2-3 cm long. Insert the shield under the bark flaps of the T-cut. Wrap with budding tape, leaving the bud exposed. After 2-3 weeks, check if the bud is green and plump. If it is, cut the rootstock about 10 cm above the bud to force the bud to grow. Remove any shoots from the rootstock below the bud. Budding is faster and uses less scion wood than grafting. It also allows you to bud many rootstocks quickly. Keep the nursery free of weeds and pests. Water regularly but avoid waterlogging. With good care, the bud will grow into a new shoot, which will become the main trunk. Budding is a skill that requires practice, but it is very rewarding.

lessons.title: Nursery Setup and Care
lessons.body: A citrus nursery should be in a sunny spot with good drainage. Prepare beds 1 meter wide and 10-20 meters long, raised 15-20 cm above ground. Mix soil with compost or well-rotted manure at a ratio of 3:1. Sterilize the soil by solarization: cover the bed with clear plastic for 4-6 weeks to kill pests and diseases. Alternatively, use fumigants if available. Sow seeds or place potted rootstocks. If using pots, use black polythene bags of 20-30 cm diameter filled with the soil mix. Space pots 30 cm apart. Water daily, preferably in the morning. Fertilize with a balanced NPK (e.g., 17-17-17) every 4-6 weeks, about 1 teaspoon per plant. Control weeds by hand weeding. Watch for pests like aphids, leaf miners, and mites. Use neem oil or recommended pesticides. For diseases like citrus canker, remove affected leaves and apply copper-based fungicide. Shade young seedlings with a shade net (50% shade) for the first 2-3 months. Harden them by gradually removing shade. Keep records of sowing, grafting, and treatments. A well-managed nursery gives healthy, vigorous seedlings ready for transplanting in 12-18 months.

lessons.title: Transplanting Seedlings to Field
lessons.body: Transplant citrus seedlings when they are 12-18 months old, 60-80 cm tall, and have a stem diameter of at least 1 cm. Choose a site with full sun and well-drained soil, pH 5.5-6.5. Prepare the field by clearing weeds and ploughing. Dig planting holes 40 cm wide and 40 cm deep, spaced 4-6 meters apart for standard trees, or 2-3 meters for dwarf varieties. Mix topsoil with 1-2 buckets of compost or manure and 100 g of phosphate fertilizer. Place the seedling in the hole, ensuring the graft union is 15-20 cm above the soil. Backfill and firm the soil. Water immediately with 10-20 liters. Mulch around the base with dry grass to conserve moisture. Stake the tree if needed. Transplant at the start of the rainy season to ensure adequate moisture. After planting, water every 2-3 days for the first month, then reduce to weekly. Protect from livestock and pests. Apply fertilizer after 2-3 months. Keep the area weed-free. With proper care, trees will start bearing fruit in 3-5 years. Transplanting is stressful for the plant, so handle roots carefully and avoid damaging the graft union.

lessons.title: Certification and Disease-Free Planting Material
lessons.body: Diseases like citrus greening (HLB), tristeza, and canker can destroy your orchard. The best way to avoid them is to plant certified disease-free seedlings. Certification means the nursery follows strict rules to produce clean plants. In many African countries, the government or authorized agencies inspect nurseries and issue certificates. Buy seedlings only from certified nurseries. Look for a label or certificate that shows the variety, rootstock, and date. Avoid buying from roadside vendors unless you know their source. To produce disease-free material, nurseries must use clean rootstock seeds, sterilized soil, and control insects that spread diseases, like psyllids for HLB. They also test mother trees for viruses. If you want to grow your own seedlings, start with certified seeds and budwood. Keep records of all treatments and inspections. Certification also ensures the variety is true to type. It may cost a little more, but it saves you from losing your entire investment. Work with your local extension officer to find certified nurseries. Remember, healthy planting material is the foundation of a profitable citrus farm.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Citrus Propagation and Nursery Management in Africa

This practical reference consolidates the core operational knowledge from the six lessons in this module. It is written for African agribusiness operators â nursery managers, commercial citrus growers, extension officers and investors â who need to move from theory to a functioning, profitable nursery. Every recommendation here is framed around the business case: certified planting material commands a price premium, reduces orchard replacement costs, and protects the long-term asset value of a citrus enterprise.

Across Africa, citrus is grown from Morocco to South Africa and from Senegal to Kenya. The dominant commercial rootstocks, the pest and disease pressures, and the certification regimes differ by region, but the propagation principles are universal. This reference brings them together in one place.

1. Seed Selection and Rootstock Varieties

Rootstock choice is the single most consequential decision in citrus propagation. It determines tree vigour, fruit quality, tolerance to soil-borne pathogens, and adaptability to local soils and climate. In Africa, the most widely used commercial rootstocks are:

Table 1: Common citrus rootstocks and their characteristics in African production systems
Rootstock Primary Use Key Strength Key Limitation
Rough lemon (Citrus jambhiri) Sweet orange, mandarin Wide soil adaptability; good in sandy soils Susceptible to citrus tristeza virus (CTV); poor salinity tolerance
Sour orange (C. aurantium) Sweet orange, grapefruit Excellent fruit quality; CTV tolerance in some strains Declining due to CTV decline strains; susceptible to Phytophthora
Carrizo citrange Sweet orange, mandarin CTV tolerant; good yield efficiency Susceptible to Phytophthora; poor in calcareous soils
Trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) Mandarin, some sweet orange Cold hardy; Phytophthora resistant Poor in high-pH soils; slow early growth
Volkameriana lemon Lemon, mandarin Vigorous; good in sandy soils Susceptible to CTV; large tree size
Citrumelo Swingle Sweet orange, grapefruit CTV tolerant; Phytophthora resistant Susceptible to citrus blight; poor in calcareous soils

Source: Cotonou & Van Vuuren (2009), Citrus Rootstocks in Southern Africa, Citrus Research International; FAO (2019), Citrus Production Manual for Smallholders.

Seed selection for rootstock production must come from certified mother trees that are free of CTV, Citrus greening (HLB), and other graft-transmissible pathogens. In Africa, where HLB is present in East Africa (Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia) and CTV is widespread, sourcing seed from a recognised certification scheme â such as the Citrus Foundation Block in South Africa or the Citrus Certification Programme in Morocco â is not optional. It is the foundation of orchard viability.

Business note: A certified rootstock seed can cost 5â10 times more than uncertified seed, but the resulting tree can produce 20â40% more marketable fruit over its lifetime and avoids the risk of whole-orchard removal. The return on investment is measured in years of production, not seed cost.

2. Grafting Techniques for Citrus

Grafting is the union of a scion (the fruiting variety) with a rootstock. In Africa, the most common methods are:

  • Whip and tongue grafting: Used for rootstocks 6â10 mm diameter. High success rate when scion and rootstock are of similar size. Best done in late winter or early spring when sap is rising.
  • Cleft grafting: Used for larger rootstocks or top-working mature trees. Suitable for changing variety in an existing orchard.
  • Side grafting: Used when rootstock is larger than scion. Common in nursery production where rootstock is grown in containers.
  • Approach grafting: Used for difficult-to-graft combinations or when a high-value scion is scarce. Labour-intensive but reliable.

Grafting success depends on: cambium contact, temperature (20â28Â°C is optimal), humidity, and hygiene. In African nurseries, where power outages and water scarcity are common, grafting should be scheduled during the cooler, wetter months to reduce desiccation risk. Sterilise tools with 70% alcohol or a 10% bleach solution between trees to prevent pathogen spread.

3. Budding Methods and Timing

Budding is preferred over grafting for large-scale commercial nursery production because it is faster, requires less scion material, and produces a cleaner union. The two main methods in Africa are:

  • T-budding (shield budding): The most common method. A single bud is inserted into a T-shaped incision in the rootstock bark. Best done when the bark slips easily â typically spring and early summer.
  • Chip budding: Used when bark is not slipping or when rootstock is small. A chip of wood with a bud is removed and fitted into a matching cut.

Timing is critical. In Southern Africa, budding is best from March to May (autumn) and September to November (spring). In East Africa, the long rains (MarchâMay) and short rains (OctoberâDecember) define the windows. Budding during extreme heat or drought stress reduces take rates dramatically.

Business note: A skilled budder can complete 300â500 buds per day. At a nursery producing 50,000 trees per year, labour for budding represents one of the largest variable costs. Training and retaining skilled budders is a competitive advantage.

4. Nursery Setup and Care

A citrus nursery must be designed to exclude pathogens and pests. Key requirements:

  • Site: Well-drained, level land, away from old citrus orchards. Minimum 100 m isolation from any citrus tree.
  • Water: Clean, pathogen-free water. Borehole or municipal water is preferred over river water.
  • Media: Sterilised potting mix (e.g., pine bark, vermiculite, sand). Never use field soil without sterilisation.
  • Containers: 4â6 litre bags or pots, raised on benches 30â50 cm above ground to prevent soil splash.
  • Shade: 30â50% shade cloth for young grafts; full sun after hardening.
  • Hygiene: Footbaths, tool sterilisation, restricted access, and regular scouting for pests and diseases.
Table 2: Nursery care schedule for citrus seedlings (0â12 months)
Stage Age (months) Key Actions Notes
Rootstock sowing 0 Sow certified seed in sterile media; keep moist at 25â30Â°C Germination in 2â4 weeks
Rootstock growth 1â6 Fertigate weekly; control weeds; monitor for aphids and mites Stem diameter should reach 5â8 mm before budding
Budding/grafting 6â8 Bud when bark slips; wrap and seal; remove rootstock suckers Take rate target: >80%
Union development 8â10 Remove wrapping after 3â4 weeks; cut back rootstock above union Force scion growth
Scion growth 10â12 Train single stem; stake if needed; continue fertigation Tree ready for field when 50â70 cm tall
Hardening 12+ Reduce shade; reduce water; expose to full sun 2â4 weeks before transplanting

Source: FAO (2019), Citrus Production Manual for Smallholders; Citrus Research International (2020), Nursery Best Management Practices.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pesticide and Pathogen Handling

Citrus nurseries in Africa frequently use copper-based fungicides, insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid) and sterilants (e.g., bleach, alcohol). These chemicals are hazardous if mishandled. Always wear gloves, eye protection and a respirator when mixing or applying. Never eat, drink or smoke during application. Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated area away from children and livestock. In areas where HLB is present, strict hygiene is a biosecurity requirement â not a suggestion. A single infected bud can destroy an entire nursery's certification status and market access.

5. Transplanting Seedlings to Field

Transplanting is the point at which nursery investment converts into orchard asset. Key steps:

  • Site preparation: Clear land, rip to 60â80 cm depth, and mark planting positions at 4â6 m spacing (depending on rootstock and variety).
  • Planting hole: 40 Ã 40 Ã 40 cm. Mix topsoil with compost and a phosphate fertiliser (e.g., 200 g superphosphate per hole).
  • Timing: Plant at the onset of rains. In irrigated systems, plant during cooler months to reduce transplant shock.
  • Handling: Remove container without disturbing roots. Set the tree at the same depth as in the nursery. Do not bury the graft union.
  • Aftercare: Water immediately; mulch; stake if windy; protect from livestock and weeds.

Business note: Transplant shock can cost 10â20% of trees in the first year. Proper hardening, timing and irrigation reduce losses to under 5%. At a tree cost of US$3â8, that is a direct saving of thousands of dollars per hectare.

6. Certification and Disease-Free Planting Material

Certification is the mechanism that guarantees a tree is true-to-type and free from graft-transmissible pathogens. In Africa, certification schemes vary by country:

  • South Africa: Citrus Foundation Block (CFB) and the Citrus Improvement Scheme (CIS).
  • Morocco: INRA certification programme.
  • Kenya: Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS) and the Citrus Certification Programme.
  • Tanzania: Tanzania Official Seed Certification Institute (TOSCI).
  • Nigeria: National Agricultural Seeds Council (NASC).

Certified trees carry a premium price but open access to formal markets, export chains and bank financing. For African agribusinesses, certification is not a cost â it is an investment in market access and asset protection.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Source rootstock seed and budwood only from certified, pathogen-tested mother trees.
  2. Match rootstock to soil type, climate and target market (fresh vs. processing).
  3. Sterilise all grafting and budding tools between trees with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach.
  4. Bud or graft when bark slips and temperatures are 20â28Â°C; avoid extreme heat or drought stress.
  5. Maintain nursery hygiene: footbaths, restricted access, raised benches, sterile media.
  6. Harden seedlings for 2â4 weeks before transplanting; plant at the onset of rains.
  7. Never bury the graft union; keep it 10â15 cm above soil level.
  8. Keep certification records for every batch â traceability is a market requirement.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Citrus Production Manual for Smallholders (2019)
  • Citrus Research International (South Africa) â Nursery Best Management Practices
  • KEPHIS â Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (Certification)
  • ISHS Acta Horticulturae â Citrus Propagation Research
  • IPPC â International Plant Protection Convention (Phytosanitary Standards)

This module is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills programme. All technical recommendations should be adapted to local conditions and regulatory requirements. Always consult your national plant protection organisation before moving citrus planting material across borders.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a rootstock in citrus propagation?
options: A) To produce the fruit variety
B) To provide the root system and influence tree size and disease resistance
C) To increase the sweetness of the fruit
D) To reduce the need for water
quiz.explanation: The rootstock provides the roots and affects the tree's vigor, size, and resistance to pests and diseases.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is known for being drought-tolerant but susceptible to some diseases?
quiz.explanation: Rough Lemon is vigorous and drought-tolerant but can be susceptible to diseases like tristeza.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for sowing citrus rootstock seeds?
quiz.explanation: Seeds should be sown 1-2 cm deep for proper germination.

quiz.q: How tall should rootstock seedlings be before grafting?
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are ready for grafting when they are 15-20 cm tall.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is resistant to tristeza virus?
quiz.explanation: Cleopatra Mandarin is resistant to tristeza and produces good quality fruit.

quiz.q: What is the most common grafting method for citrus?
quiz.explanation: Cleft grafting is widely used for citrus when the rootstock is 1-2 cm thick.

quiz.q: When is the best time to graft citrus?
options: B) At the start of the rainy season
C) In the middle of winter
quiz.explanation: Grafting is best done during active growth, which occurs at the start of the rainy season.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of wrapping the graft union with tape?
options: B) To hold the scion and rootstock together and prevent drying
quiz.explanation: The tape holds the graft in place and reduces moisture loss, aiding the healing process.

quiz.q: How long does it take to see new growth after grafting?
quiz.explanation: New growth typically appears within 2-3 weeks if the graft is successful.

quiz.q: What tool is essential for grafting?
quiz.explanation: A sharp knife is needed to make clean cuts for grafting.

quiz.q: What is T-budding also known as?
quiz.explanation: T-budding is also called shield budding because the bud piece resembles a shield.

quiz.q: When is the best time to do budding?
options: A) When the bark slips easily
B) When the tree is dormant
quiz.explanation: Budding is most successful when the bark slips easily, which is during active growth.

quiz.q: How thick should the rootstock be for T-budding?
quiz.explanation: Rootstock is usually ready for budding when it is about 1 cm thick.

quiz.q: After a successful bud take, what should you do to the rootstock?
options: A) Cut it back above the bud
quiz.explanation: Cutting the rootstock above the bud forces the bud to grow into a new shoot.

quiz.q: What is an advantage of budding over grafting?
options: A) It uses less scion wood
B) It is easier for beginners
C) It works on thicker rootstocks
quiz.explanation: Budding requires only a single bud, so less scion wood is needed.

quiz.q: What is the ideal width for a citrus nursery bed?
quiz.explanation: Beds should be 1 meter wide for easy access and management.

quiz.q: How can you sterilize nursery soil?
options: A) By solarization with clear plastic
quiz.explanation: Solarization using clear plastic for 4-6 weeks kills pests and diseases in the soil.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for potted rootstocks in the nursery?
quiz.explanation: Pots should be spaced 30 cm apart to allow air circulation and prevent competition.

quiz.q: How often should you fertilize nursery seedlings with NPK?
quiz.explanation: A balanced NPK fertilizer should be applied every 4-6 weeks for healthy growth.

quiz.q: What percentage shade is recommended for young seedlings?
quiz.explanation: 50% shade net protects young seedlings from intense sun without completely blocking light.

quiz.q: When are citrus seedlings ready for transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are typically ready for transplanting at 12-18 months when they are 60-80 cm tall.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for standard citrus trees?
quiz.explanation: Standard trees need 4-6 meters spacing to allow for canopy growth.

quiz.q: Where should the graft union be positioned when transplanting?
quiz.explanation: The graft union should be 15-20 cm above the soil to prevent rootstock from rooting and to avoid disease.

quiz.q: What is the best time to transplant citrus seedlings?
options: A) Start of the rainy season
B) Middle of the dry season
C) End of the rainy season
quiz.explanation: Transplanting at the start of the rainy season ensures adequate moisture for establishment.

quiz.q: How much water should be given immediately after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: 10-20 liters of water helps settle the soil around the roots and reduce transplant shock.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of using certified disease-free seedlings?
options: C) They are free from diseases like HLB and tristeza
quiz.explanation: Certified seedlings are tested and grown under strict conditions to ensure they are disease-free.

quiz.q: Which disease is spread by psyllids and is a major threat to citrus?
quiz.explanation: Citrus greening (HLB) is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid and is devastating to citrus.

quiz.q: What should you look for when buying certified seedlings?
options: A) A label or certificate with variety and rootstock details
quiz.explanation: Certified seedlings come with a label or certificate indicating their variety, rootstock, and health status.

quiz.q: Why is certification important for citrus nurseries?
options: B) It ensures plants are true to type and disease-free
C) It reduces the cost of production
D) It allows the use of any soil
quiz.explanation: Certification ensures that the planting material is genetically true to type and free from regulated diseases.

quiz.q: What is the first step to produce disease-free planting material?
options: A) Use certified seeds and budwood
B) Use soil from the field
quiz.explanation: Starting with certified seeds and budwood is essential to avoid introducing diseases.
